C002.subject: trade liberalization in developing nations
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: trade liberalization in developing nations within-country income inequality]

[PATH:empirical] Household Income and Expenditure Surveys (HIES) and labor force surveys from Indonesia, Mexico, and Vietnam, combined with tariff data from the World Bank's World Integrated Trade Solution (WITS) database — Panel data analysis of household-level income inequality indices (e.g., Gini, Theil) before and after major trade liberalization episodes in the post-1990s period can provide direct causal estimates using difference-in-differences or event-study designs, particularly within low-skill manufacturing sectors in East Asia and Latin America.

[PATH:literature] Goldberg, P. K., & Pavcnik, N. (2007). 'Distributional Effects of Globalization in Developing Countries.' Journal of Economic Literature, 45(1), 39-82. — This comprehensive survey synthesizes empirical evidence on the relationship between trade liberalization and inequality in developing nations, highlighting heterogeneous effects across skill groups and sectors. It provides a theoretical framework and key references for assessing whether tariff reductions in low-skill manufacturing narrow or widen income gaps.

[PATH:theoretical] Melitz, M. J. (2003). 'The Impact of Trade on Intra-Industry Reallocations and Aggregate Industry Productivity.' Econometrica, 71(6), 1695-1725. — This seminal model of firm heterogeneity in trade offers a theoretical basis for predicting that trade liberalization may increase within-industry wage dispersion if only high-productivity firms (often skill-intensive) benefit, potentially countering the hypothesis in low-skill sectors. Extensions incorporating skill premia can guide empirical tests.

C005.object: within-country income inequality in developing nations with weak social safety nets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: economic globalization within-country income inequality in developing nations with weak social safety nets]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on trade liberalization and Gini coefficients across developing countries with weak social safety nets, focusing on high-skill service sector employment shares — Directly tests whether increased globalization in high-skill services correlates with rising within-country inequality under low institutional capacity, using cross-country time-series variation.

[PATH:empirical] Case studies of service sector outsourcing hubs (e.g., India, Philippines) examining wage dispersion between high-skill and low-skill workers, controlling for social safety net strength — Provides micro-level evidence on the mechanism linking globalization to inequality, while isolating the role of weak safety nets in amplifying disparities.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of trade with heterogeneous firms and institutional frictions (e.g., Melitz-style models extended for service sectors and institutional quality) — Clarifies the causal channels through which low institutional capacity moderates the effect of globalization on inequality, helping to interpret empirical findings and refine the hypothesis.

C008.subject: economic globalization
C008.predicate: has heterogeneous effects on within-country income inequality in developing nations with weak social safety nets, depending on the sector composition of globalization
C008.object: within-country income inequality in developing nations with weak social safety nets
evidence_refs: [SYNTHESIS] The apparent contradiction is resolved by recognizing that the overall effect of globalization masks sector-specific dynamics: low-skill manufacturing or commodity flows may reduce inequality by raising wages for lower-income groups (Branch A), while globalization in high-skill service sectors disproportionately benefits higher-income groups, widening inequality (Branch B). Thus, the net impact depends on which sectors dominate a nation's globalization profile.
